elements.brief_element: The subsystem provides reliable webhook delivery.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction describes “A durable webhook-delivery system” and recovers ingress, fan-out, delivery, retries, dead letters, replay, status, and metrics.
elements.note: The system’s overall purpose is explicit and accurate.

elements.brief_element: The webhook delivery subsystem is multi-tenant.
elements.brief_evidence: “We are building a multi-tenant webhook delivery subsystem.”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The system purpose refers to “tenant secrets” and “tenant-visible history”; the components include “Active tenant secret” and “Tenant-visible status history.”
elements.note: Tenant-specific secret and status ownership make the multi-tenant boundary recoverable.

elements.brief_element: The primary end-to-end flow is product services → internal ingress API → durable event record and acknowledgement → dispatcher fan-out → durable delivery queue → delivery worker signing and customer call → completion, retry, or dead-letter outcome.
elements.brief_evidence: “Product services publish webhook events through an internal ingress API… A dispatcher expands the event into one delivery per subscribed endpoint and puts those deliveries on a durable queue. Delivery workers… sign the exact payload, and call the customer endpoint… A 2xx response completes the delivery… [failures] return through a retry scheduler… Permanent failures and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter queue.”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction provides ordered flows titled “Durable event ingestion,” “Fan-out and endpoint-state evaluation,” “Normal webhook delivery,” “Retry loop,” and “Dead-letter routing,” connecting Product services, Internal ingress API, Durable event record, Dispatcher, Durable delivery queue, Delivery worker, Customer endpoint, completion, retry, and dead-letter handling.
elements.note: The overall architecture and main operating sequence are recoverable, although individual details within the flow have losses recorded below.

elements.brief_element: Product services publish webhook events.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “Product services” component is described as originating and publishing events, and “Durable event ingestion” begins with “Product services publish an event.”
elements.note: Source and action are clear.

elements.brief_element: Product services publish events through an internal ingress API.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction identifies an “Internal ingress API” that accepts published events, with the ordered sequence “Product services” → “publish event” → “Internal ingress API.”
elements.note: The ingress ownership and direction are correct.

elements.brief_element: The ingress transaction durably records every accepted event.
elements.brief_evidence: “…the ingress transaction must durably record each accepted event…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “Durable event record” component persists an accepted event, and the ingestion flow says the event is “persisted transactionally as a Durable event record.”
elements.note: Transactional durability at ingress is explicitly recovered.

elements.brief_element: Ingress acknowledges acceptance only after the event has been durably recorded.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The flow places “Acknowledge accepted” after “Durable event record” through a connector labeled “durable”; the constraints state “Ingress acceptance occurs only after durable persistence.”
elements.note: The critical durability-before-acknowledgement ordering is one of the clearest transmitted behaviors.

elements.brief_element: A dispatcher processes the durable event.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “Dispatcher” receives a flow from the Durable event record and is described as consuming durable event records.
elements.note: Dispatcher placement and input are clear.

elements.brief_element: The dispatcher expands each event according to endpoint subscriptions.
elements.brief_evidence: “A dispatcher expands the event into one delivery per subscribed endpoint…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The Dispatcher responsibility says it performs fan-out by “expanding subscriptions,” and the fan-out flow consults “Subscriptions + endpoint config + rate limit.”
elements.note: Subscription-based expansion is recovered.

elements.brief_element: The dispatcher creates exactly one delivery per subscribed endpoint.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction says the Dispatcher “fan[s] them out by expanding subscriptions,” but no reconstruction entry explicitly states the one-delivery-per-subscribed-endpoint cardinality.
elements.note: Fan-out is clear, but the exact delivery cardinality is not.

elements.brief_element: The dispatcher places generated deliveries on a durable queue.
elements.brief_evidence: “…and puts those deliveries on a durable queue.”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: A “Durable delivery queue” is described as durably queuing deliveries ready for the delivery loop, downstream of dispatcher and endpoint-state evaluation.
elements.note: The durable handoff from fan-out to workers is recoverable.

elements.brief_element: Delivery workers consume queued deliveries.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “Delivery worker” processes queued deliveries, and “Normal webhook delivery” begins with “A queued delivery reaches the Delivery worker.”
elements.note: Worker responsibility and queue relationship are clear.

elements.brief_element: For each delivery, the worker loads the tenant’s active signing secret.
elements.brief_evidence: “Delivery workers load the tenant's active signing secret…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction identifies an “Active secret” component that provides the “active tenant secret used for delivery signing,” and the normal delivery flow selects it before signing.
elements.note: Active-secret selection and tenant ownership are both recovered.

elements.brief_element: The worker signs the exact payload.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: A component is explicitly named “Sign exact payload,” and the constraints repeat that the exact payload is signed.
elements.note: Payload-signing semantics are exact.

elements.brief_element: The worker calls the customer endpoint.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The normal delivery flow sends the signed payload to the “Customer endpoint,” which is described as receiving the webhook delivery.
elements.note: The destination and call direction are clear.

elements.brief_element: The customer endpoint call includes an idempotency key.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: No matching reconstruction entry mentions an idempotency key or states that one is included in the customer request.
elements.note: This delivery-safety contract is absent.

elements.brief_element: A 2xx customer response completes the delivery.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “2xx response?” decision has a green route to “Complete delivery,” and the normal delivery flow explicitly says a 2xx result completes delivery.
elements.note: Success classification and terminal outcome are exact.

elements.brief_element: Timeouts are routed through the retry scheduler.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The retry-policy component explicitly names “Timeouts,” and the associated failure path routes such outcomes through the Retry scheduler.
elements.note: The retry-policy note settles inclusion of timeouts despite the branch label only saying retryable/network.

elements.brief_element: Network failures are routed through the retry scheduler.
elements.brief_evidence: “…network failures… return through a retry scheduler…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The response branch is labeled “retryable / network” and leads to “Retry scheduler”; the retry-policy note also explicitly names network failures.
elements.note: Trigger and route are both visible.

elements.brief_element: Retryable responses are routed through the retry scheduler.
elements.brief_evidence: “…retryable responses return through a retry scheduler…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “retryable / network” branch reaches “Retry scheduler,” and the retry-policy note explicitly includes retryable responses.
elements.note: Retryable-response routing is clear.

elements.brief_element: The retry scheduler uses exponential backoff.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The Retry policy says “exponential backoff + jitter,” and the retry-loop flow applies backoff before checking attempts.
elements.note: The scheduling algorithm is explicit.

elements.brief_element: The retry scheduler adds jitter to retry timing.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The Retry policy explicitly says “exponential backoff + jitter.”
elements.note: Jitter is directly recovered.

elements.brief_element: Retrying is bounded by a maximum attempt count.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction includes “Attempts remain?” and a note ending in “with a maximum...,” but its uncertainty list says it cannot determine whether this is a maximum delay, maximum attempt count, or another maximum.
elements.note: A bounded retry loop is apparent, but the specific maximum-attempt-count constraint is not conclusively communicated.

elements.brief_element: When attempts remain, the delivery is returned to the delivery worker for another attempt.
elements.brief_evidence: “Timeouts, network failures, and retryable responses return through a retry scheduler…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The Retry loop checks “Attempts remain?” and, when attempts remain, loops back to the Delivery worker.
elements.note: The retry feedback loop and ordering are recoverable.

elements.brief_element: Permanent failures go directly to the dead-letter queue rather than being retried.
elements.brief_evidence: “Permanent failures… go to a dead-letter queue…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: No matching reconstruction entry identifies a permanent or non-retryable failure trigger. The reconstruction explicitly says the red dead-letter path’s trigger cannot be determined and may represent non-retryable responses, exhausted attempts, or both.
elements.note: The permanent-failure branch and its direct terminal route are not recoverable.

elements.brief_element: Deliveries whose retries are exhausted go to the dead-letter queue.
elements.brief_evidence: “…and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter queue…”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The “Attempts remain?” decision has an outbound path associated with dead-letter handling, but the reconstruction states that the branch label is not visible and the exact dead-letter trigger cannot be determined.
elements.note: The topology strongly suggests exhausted-attempt routing, but the judge correctly could not establish it unambiguously.

elements.brief_element: The dead-letter queue preserves the payload.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The dead-letter preservation note explicitly lists “Payload” under “Preserved intact.”
elements.note: Payload preservation is exact.

elements.brief_element: The dead-letter queue preserves the endpoint.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The dead-letter preservation note explicitly lists “endpoint.”
elements.note: Endpoint preservation is exact.

elements.brief_element: The dead-letter queue preserves the attempt history.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The dead-letter preservation note explicitly lists “attempt history.”
elements.note: Attempt-history preservation is exact.

elements.brief_element: The dead-letter queue preserves the last error.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The dead-letter preservation note explicitly lists “last error.”
elements.note: Last-error preservation is exact.

elements.brief_element: Operators can inspect dead-lettered deliveries.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction identifies an “Operator” and an “Inspect delivery” operation adjacent to the Dead-letter queue.
elements.note: Actor and operation are explicit.

elements.brief_element: Operators can replay dead-lettered deliveries.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction contains “Operator,” “Inspect delivery,” and “Replay delivery,” with an orange replay path returning toward the delivery system.
elements.note: Replay capability is clear even though the exact re-entry component is ambiguous.

elements.brief_element: Replaying a dead-lettered delivery does not change its original event identity.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The replay path is explicitly labeled “replay · same event identity,” and the constraints repeat that replay uses the same event identity.
elements.note: Identity preservation across replay is exact.

elements.brief_element: Endpoint configuration can be paused.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction includes endpoint configuration and an “Endpoint paused?” decision.
elements.note: Pause state is represented as endpoint configuration.

elements.brief_element: Paused endpoints retain their deliveries rather than dropping or delivering them.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The paused-endpoint failure path says the delivery is held until resume, and the policy note says resume releases paused deliveries. The reconstruction acknowledges that the intermediate holding component is unlabeled.
elements.note: Retention behavior is recoverable, though storage ownership is visually ambiguous.

elements.brief_element: Retained deliveries remain paused until the endpoint is resumed.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction states “The delivery is held until resume,” and the normal branch is labeled “no / resumed.”
elements.note: The release condition is clear.

elements.brief_element: Resuming an endpoint releases its retained deliveries back into delivery processing.
elements.brief_evidence: “…paused endpoints retain deliveries until they are resumed.”
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction quotes the policy note: “Resume releases paused deliveries into the endpoint allowance check.”
elements.note: Resume behavior is explicit; the added allowance check is an unsupported extension recorded separately.

elements.brief_element: Every delivery attempt feeds tenant-visible status history.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The status update rule says “Every delivery attempt and outcome updates both views,” one of which is “Tenant-visible status history.”
elements.note: Attempt reporting and tenant visibility are explicit.

elements.brief_element: Every delivery outcome feeds tenant-visible status history.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The status update rule explicitly states that every outcome updates “Tenant-visible status history.”
elements.note: Outcome reporting is exact.

elements.brief_element: Every delivery attempt feeds operational metrics.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The status update rule says every delivery attempt updates both views, including “Operational metrics.”
elements.note: Attempt-level metrics are explicit.

elements.brief_element: Every delivery outcome feeds operational metrics.
elements.reconstruction_evidence: The status update rule says every delivery outcome updates both views, including “Operational metrics.”
elements.note: Outcome-level metrics are explicit.

unsupported_claims.claim: Endpoint configuration includes rate-limit state and deliveries must pass an endpoint allowance check.
unsupported_claims.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction identifies “Subscriptions + endpoint config + rate limit” and an “Endpoint allowance...” decision.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: The brief defines pause state but does not mention endpoint rate limits, allowance checks, quotas, or throttling.

unsupported_claims.claim: Over-limit deliveries enter a dedicated durable rate-limit wait queue.
unsupported_claims.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction describes an “Endpoint allowance...” branch labeled “no · wait” leading to a “Durable rate-limit wait queue.”
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: The brief specifies only the dispatcher’s durable delivery queue and paused-delivery retention; it does not define an over-limit path or a separate rate-limit queue.

unsupported_claims.claim: Resumed paused deliveries must pass through the endpoint allowance check.
unsupported_claims.reconstruction_evidence: The reconstruction states, “Resume releases paused deliveries into the endpoint allowance check.”
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: The brief says paused deliveries are retained until resume, but it does not prescribe a rate-limit or allowance stage after resumption.

unsupported_claims.claim: Ingress must transactionally persist a stable event identity as a separately explicit field before acknowledgement.
unsupported_claims.reconstruction_evidence: The transactional-boundary component and constraints state that “the exact event payload and stable event identity” must be persisted transactionally.
unsupported_claims.why_unsupported: The brief requires durable recording of each accepted event and preservation of original event identity during replay, but it does not explicitly specify a separate stable-identity persistence field or this exact transactional data contract.

verdict.strongest_transmitted_behavior: The durability-first ingress sequence is transmitted exceptionally well: product services publish through the internal ingress API, the event is transactionally persisted as a durable record, and acceptance is acknowledged only after durability.
verdict.most_consequential_loss: The request idempotency key is entirely absent, and the dead-letter trigger semantics do not clearly distinguish permanent failures from exhausted retries. Together these omissions weaken both duplicate-delivery safety and the actionable failure-routing contract.
verdict.overall_summary: The reconstruction accurately conveys the purpose, ownership boundaries, major components, primary end-to-end flow, signing behavior, 2xx completion, retry loop, dead-letter record contents, operator replay with unchanged event identity, pause retention, and status/metrics reporting. It is strong enough for an engineering design discussion. However, it omits the idempotency key, only partially communicates the exact one-delivery-per-endpoint cardinality and maximum-attempt constraint, and leaves permanent-failure versus exhausted-retry routing ambiguous. It also introduces a substantial endpoint-rate-limiting subsystem not present in the brief. These losses prevent the board from being a complete implementation specification but do not contradict the main architecture.
